analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set minimum registered-nurse staffing levels and post them publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that takes Medicare patients to adopt a staffing system guaranteeing enough registered nurses on each shift and in each unit. Hospitals would have to post daily staffing numbers where patients could see them, submit staffing data to the government, keep records, and face fines up to $10,000 per violation. It also included whistleblower protections so nurses and patients who complained about staffing could not be punished.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be cared for by more registered nurses — research cited in the bill links patient health directly to nurse staffing levels [S3]. Registered nurses would also gain, since the staffing system must be built on input from direct-care nurses and the bill protects nurses who report unsafe staffing from retaliation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires each Medicare-participating hospital to adopt a staffing system ensuring enough registered nurses on every shift and in every unit, with nurse-to-patient ratios that can only adjust upward based on patient needs [S2][S3].

Requires hospitals to post daily, in a visible place, the number of licensed and unlicensed nursing staff on each unit, and requires the Health and Human Services Department to publish the data online [S3].
Sets civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation — higher for hospitals with a pattern of violations — and publicly names penalized hospitals on an HHS website [S3].

Bars hospitals from retaliating against nurses or patients who file staffing complaints, and lets prevailing employees win reinstatement and back pay, and patients $5,000 in liquidated damages, in federal court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would bear the cost of hiring more registered nurses, building staffing systems, daily public reporting, and recordkeeping, plus fines for violations. To the extent Medicare payments do not cover those added costs, some of it could show up in hospital budgets and, indirectly, in broader health care prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals that employ too few nurses

drawbacks.text: Staffing mandates are expensive for hospitals, and the bill does not include dedicated funding for the added nursing labor; hospitals would bear hiring costs that could pressure margins, particularly for rural and safety-net hospitals.

The bill relies on flexible, hospital-designed staffing systems rather than a single fixed ratio, so its strength would depend heavily on how the Secretary wrote regulations and how strictly hospitals were audited.
The United States already had a declared nursing shortage when the bill was introduced, so a mandate to employ more nurses could have been hard to meet quickly in some markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the stakes are safety: the bill's own findings cite studies linking patient outcomes directly to the number of registered nurses on duty. The costs fall on hospitals, the party whose understaffing the bill targets, and the design leaves hospitals flexibility in how they meet the requirement while requiring public reporting and penalties. The main honest concern is cost pressure on hospitals without new funding, and enforcement hinging on future regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it once and sent it to the Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Inouye introduced the Registered Nurse Safe Staffing Act of 2005 on January 24, 2005 [S1][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the only further action was a 'Star Print ordered' on February 9, 2005, a technical reprint [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor in the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals came out ahead: they avoided mandatory nurse staffing systems, daily public staffing disclosure, and fines of up to $10,000 per violation. Patients and nurses gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 24, 2005 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so the partisan split is unknown; the bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required hospitals to hire and schedule more registered nurses, post staffing levels publicly, and pay fines up to $10,000 per violation. Hospitals' interest in keeping staffing lean runs against patient safety, the bill's stated purpose.
The bill requires staffing systems built on input from direct-care nurses and specialty nursing organizations, and protects nurses who complain about staffing from retaliation.
